name: Grand Canal of China
info: The Grand Canal is a system of linked canals joining rivers and lakes in North and East China, begun with the Han Canal in 486 BCE, completed by Emperor Yang of Sui in 609 and used as a north–south artery for some fourteen centuries.

facts.made: Built in stages over many centuries: the Han Canal for King Fuchai of Wu from 486 BCE, the Sui network under Emperor Yang by conscripted labour, then summit sections under the Yuan and a renovation under the Ming
facts.form: A system of canals, canalised rivers and lakes; the main Jing–Hang stem is thought to extend for 1,776 km from Beijing to Hangzhou, in six main subsections, with a single summit section and pound locks
facts.where: Across Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shandong and Hebei and the municipalities of Tianjin and Beijing, from Hangzhou on the Qiantang River to Tongzhou on the edge of Beijing, with the Eastern Zhejiang Canal to Ningbo
facts.known: the longest artificial waterway in the world; the Sui network of 604 to 609; the grain shipments to the north; the pound lock; the summit sections of the Yuan; its use as the eastern route of the South-North Water Diversion Project; its World Heritage listing in 2014

t: The oldest sections were dug in the early 5th century BCE for the states of Wu and Yue, and Emperor Yang of Sui joined and extended them between 604 and 609 to link Jiangnan with his capital and his armies, using massive levies of conscripted labour.
For centuries the canal carried the grain collected in taxes from the Yangtze Delta to the north, and each dynasty treated its repair and the control of the Yellow River's floods as a duty.

Floods, wars and the shifting of the Yellow River repeatedly broke the canal, and after 1855 its northern and southern parts stayed separate for decades; it was rebuilt after 1949, and UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2014.
dyk: By the year 735 about 150 million kilograms of grain were recorded as shipped each year along the canal, and in the mid-15th century 121,500 soldiers and officers were needed simply to operate its 11,775 government grain barges.
ev: King Fuchai of Wu began the Han Canal, which within three years connected the Yangtze with the Huai River
Emperor Yang of Sui completed the network after levies of conscripted labour, begun in 604, linking Yangzhou, Luoyang, Suzhou and Hangzhou and the northeast
Qiao Weiyue, an Assistant Commissioner of Transport for Huainan, invented the double-gate pound lock
Kaifeng's governor Du Chong broke the dykes holding back the Yellow River against the Jurchen, and the floods ruined much of the canal
A summit section was dug across the foothills of the Shandong massif, linking Hangzhou and Beijing by a direct waterway for the first time
The Ming renovated the canal almost entirely in the years to 1415, using 165,000 labourers in Shandong
The Yellow River flooded and changed its course, severing the canal in Shandong
UNESCO's World Heritage Conference listed the Grand Canal as a World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
The Grand Canal is a system of interconnected canals linking major rivers and lakes in North and East China. It served as an important waterborne transport route between the north and the south in medieval and premodern China. Its oldest sections were completed in the early 5th century BCE, during the conflicts of the Spring and Autumn period, to provide supplies and transport routes for the states of Wu and Yue. King Fuchai of Wu, whose capital was in present-day Suzhou, ventured north to attack the State of Qi and ordered a canal built for trade and to ship supplies north in case his forces should engage the northern states of Song and Lu. This became the Han Canal. Work began in 486 BCE south of Yangzhou, and within three years it had connected the Yangtze with the Huai River, using existing waterways, lakes and marshes.

The Han Canal is known as the second oldest section, since the Hong Canal most likely preceded it. The Hong Canal linked the Yellow River near Kaifeng to the Si and Bian rivers and became the model for the shape of the canal in the north. Its date is uncertain. The diplomat Su Qin first mentioned it in 330 BCE, Sima Qian knew of no historical date for it and discussed it just after the legendary works of Yu the Great, and modern scholars now consider it to belong to the 6th century BCE. The Eastern Zhejiang Canal began as the Shanyin Canal, excavated in Shaoxing by the Yue official Fan Li in the early 5th century BCE.
sections.content:
The main stem, the Jing–Hang Grand Canal, is thought to extend for 1,776 km, linking Beijing in the north to Hangzhou in the south, and is divided into six main subsections. The Jiangnan Canal runs from the Qiantang River at Hangzhou around the east side of Lake Tai, through Jiaxing, Suzhou and Wuxi, to the Yangtze at Zhenjiang. The Inner Canal runs from Yangzhou to the Huai River at Huai'an, and the Middle Canal from Huai'an to Luoma Lake and then to the Nansi Lakes. The Lu Canal continues through Shandong to the Wei at Linqing, the Southern Canal runs from Linqing to the Hai River at Tianjin, and the Northern Canal runs from Tianjin to Tongzhou on the outskirts of Beijing. The route passes through the provinces of Zhejiang, Jiangsu, Shandong and Hebei and the municipalities of Tianjin and Beijing. In 2014 the Eastern Zhejiang Canal from Hangzhou to Ningbo was also recognised as an official component.

Though the canal nominally crosses the watersheds of five river systems, the variation between them is so low that it has only a single summit section. The water flows from Beijing toward Tianjin, from Nanwang north toward Tianjin and from Nanwang south toward Yangzhou. The canal did not form a single continuous man-made channel but used artificial channels together with canalised and natural waterways. Along the Sui canals ran an imperial roadway with stables at regular intervals for a rapid courier system, and lines of trees were planted along parts of the canal as windbreaks.
sections.making:
The reunification of China under the Sui dynasty ended three centuries of chaos and allowed the repair of existing canals and the construction of new ones. Their main purpose was to tap the resources of Jiangnan in the southeast to enrich the capital at Luoyang and to supply the Sui armies in the Goguryeo–Sui War. A levee project of 587 under the engineer Liang Rui established lock gates to regulate water levels. By 600 silt had built up in the Hong Canal, and the chief engineer Yuwen Kai advised digging a new canal parallel to it. With the recorded labour of five million people under the supervision of Ma Shumou, the first major section, the Bian Qu, was completed in 605. The whole network was completed between 604 and 609 under Emperor Yang, again with massive levies of conscripted labour, as the Record of the Opening of the Canal describes at length.

Later builders added to it. The Mongol Oqruqči engineered the Jizhou Canal in 1238 as the first true summit section, and the Huitong Canal was built in 1289 by the engineer Ma Zhizhen after a geological survey. A summit section dug across the foothills of the Shandong massif in the 1280s shortened the overall length by as much as 700 km. Between 1411 and 1415 the Ming dammed the Wen River to feed 60% of its water north into the canal, dug four large reservoirs in Shandong, and used 165,000 labourers to dredge the bed and build new channels, embankments and locks. In 984 Qiao Weiyue invented the pound lock, which let ships wait in a gated space while the water was drained to the right level.
sections.reception:
The Tang capital at Chang'an was the most thriving metropolis of China in its day, but the city of Yangzhou, close to the canal, was the economic hub of the era, as headquarters of the government salt monopoly and the largest pre-modern industrial production centre of the empire. One of the greatest benefits of the canal in the Tang and later dynasties was that it reduced the cost of shipping tax grain from the Yangtze Delta to northern China. Officials in charge of the canal and nearby salt works grew enormously wealthy. The canal played a major role in periodically reuniting northern and southern China, and in the Ming dynasty it made or broke the fortunes of cities along its route: Suzhou, better placed on the main artery than Nanjing or Hangzhou, became Ming China's greatest economic centre.

The costs fell on those who built and ran it. The unpopular Goguryeo–Sui War and the massive civil conscription involved in creating the canals were among the chief factors in the rebellions of Emperor Yang's reign and the rapid fall of the Sui. The scholar Gu Yanwu estimated that the Ming had to employ 47,004 full-time labourers recruited by the lijia corvée system to maintain the canal. Travellers admired it, among them the monk Ennin, Marco Polo, Rashid al-Din Hamadani, Ibn Battuta, the Korean official Choe Bu, who travelled its whole length in 1488, and the missionary Matteo Ricci. In 1169 the Southern Song envoy Lou Yue recorded his journey north along it in a diary.
sections.survival:
The canal's history is one of damage and repair. Sections degraded during the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms period and the Song dynasty, and periodic flooding of the Yellow River eroded and threatened it; during wars the rivers' high dikes were sometimes deliberately breached. In 858 an enormous flood along the canal inundated thousands of acres of farmland and killed tens of thousands of people. After 1128, when Du Chong broke the dykes and dams against the Jurchen invaders, a series of floods shifted the Yellow River south of Shandong, and much of the canal was ruined for several years. Even so, restoration of the canal and its flood control works was assumed as a duty by each successive dynasty. A Chinese official remarked in 1447 that the flood-prone Yellow River made the canal like a throat that could easily be strangled.

In 1855 the Yellow River flooded and changed course, severing the canal in Shandong, and the dikes were opened to flood the advancing troops of the Taiping Rebellion's Northern Expedition. The difficulty of crossing the Yellow River, a sea route for grain ships and the opening of the Tianjin–Pukou and Beijing–Hankou railways left the canal to languish, and for decades its northern and southern parts stayed separate. Some sections fell into disrepair and some were returned to flat fields. After 1949 the authorities ordered heavy reconstruction, and the portion south of the Yellow River remains in heavy use by barges carrying bulk cargo, including coal, sand and construction materials.
sections.legacy:
The Grand Canal has been upgraded to serve as the eastern route of the South-North Water Diversion Project, which pumps water from the Yangtze at Jiangdu near Yangzhou, repumps it through 23 stations to the watershed at Nanwang and carries it by gravity to reservoirs in Tianjin. Industrialisation left the canal greatly polluted: by the 1990s barge crews could tell when they neared Hangzhou by the stench of the black water, and fishermen on Dongping Lake objected when water from the Yangtze appeared to kill fish. In the 21st century efforts to improve conditions have increased. Around Hangzhou a $250 million restoration project begun in 2001 improved water quality until the water no longer produced a noticeable odor and could support some fauna.

On 22 June 2014 UNESCO's World Heritage Conference listed the Grand Canal as a World Heritage Site, a complex of 31 sections and a number of accessory heritage sites. The China Grand Canal Museum opened in 2021. Within China the canal is credited with enabling cultural exchange and political integration between north and south and with serving as the economic lifeline of indigenous trade, and rulers used it for tours of inspection: the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors made twelve trips to the south, on all occasions but one reaching Hangzhou. At Tongzhou, where the modern canal stops, a Grand Canal Cultural Park has been built.

summary: The Grand Canal is a system of linked canals in North and East China, begun with the Han Canal in 486 BCE and completed by Emperor Yang of Sui in 609. It carried grain and trade between north and south for centuries, was broken by floods and shifts of the Yellow River, and was listed as a World Heritage Site in 2014.
notes: Length: the lead gives 1,776 km for the Jing–Hang stem, the Modern course section 1,794 km nominally; I used 1,776 km (thought to) in the text and the facts box.
Summit height: the lead and the Jizhou Canal section say 42 m (the latter 'above the Yangtze'), the Lu Canal and Elevations sections 38.5 m; I left the figure out.

Navigable extent today: the Modern course section says only Hangzhou to Liangshan is navigable, the Transportation section says ships can only go up to Jining; left out. Only the Jiangnan-to-Yellow-River statement 'the portion south of the Yellow River remains in heavy use' (lead) is used.

The Jia Canal section dates Li Hualong's canal to 12 BC and then says by 1688 the Middle Canal by Jin Fu removed the Yellow River stretch: the date is evidently wrong (a 'BC' for a later work); the section is left out.

Mongol dates: the Jizhou Canal is said to be engineered in 1238 (Oqruqči), the lead and Yuan section say a summit section was dug in the 1280s; both given as the article has them. The article's Yuan section and the Jizhou section call the summit 'rose to a height of 42 m above the Yangtze' versus above sea level in the lead; figure omitted.
Pound lock: lead says invented in the 10th century; Song section says 984; I used 984.

Left out: the paragraph on the Erie Canal (influence on western works), which is thinly sourced and contradicts nothing but claims direct design inspiration; the Lake Lianhu paragraph (garbled English); the 'Yilou Canal', 'Duke Huan's Conduit' and 'Nanyang New Canal' details; the 2012 dredging target ('will likely continue'); 2019 plans for Tai'an.
Date of construction 'start' -486 with circa true: the article gives 486 BC for the Han Canal and 'early 5th century BC' for the oldest sections.
The Tang figure of 149,685,400 kilograms is given in the article as '165,000 short tons'; the article's own conversion is used.
